summary: Describes the routing architecture of the NSFNET, centered on the new NSFNET Backbone. It focuses on the interface between the backbone and the networks attached to it.

plainLanguage.summary: A big highway connects many smaller towns. This explains how the highway and the town roads agree on where traffic should go.

subtitle: How the national science network backbone talked to regional networks

tldr.problem: The newly built NSFNET Backbone needed a routing architecture to connect to regional university and research networks while managing routing information consistently and securely.
tldr.mechanism: The backbone uses a Shortest Path First interior routing protocol internally and Exterior Gateway Protocol (EGP) at the boundary with regional networks. Routing policies enforce strict filtering and validation of routing announcements to prevent loops and ensure consistent routing databases.
tldr.outcome: The NSFNET Backbone became the core of the US research internet, connecting dozens of regional networks with defined and enforced routing policies that prevented routing chaos.

today: RFC 1093 is an informational document describing the NSFNET Backbone as it existed in 1989. The NSFNET itself has since been decommissioned and replaced by commercial Internet Service Providers (ISPs) and academic network infrastructures. However, the routing architecture and policy enforcement principles it describes remain relevant to modern Internet routing design.

sections.title: The NSFNET Backbone Architecture
sections.content:
The National Science Foundation built a new backbone network in the late 1980s to connect the US research and education community. The NSFNET Backbone, also called the "New NSFNET Backbone," forms the core of the overall NSFNET and connects to regional networks (also called regional backbones), peer networks (such as ARPANET and the NASA Science Network), and individual campus networks.

This document describes how routing works in this architecture, with specific emphasis on the interface between the backbone and the networks attached to it. The core uses a Shortest Path First (SPF) based interior routing protocol adapted from the IS-IS protocol. The boundaries with regional networks use the Exterior Gateway Protocol (EGP), which has been extended with new capabilities for policy-based routing.
sections.plainLanguage: The backbone is the main highway. Inside the backbone, routers all know about each other and agree on the best paths. At the edges where regional networks connect, a different protocol handles the handoff so each region can manage its own traffic.

sections.title: Interior and Exterior Routing
sections.content:
The NSFNET Backbone uses two routing protocols working together. Inside the backbone, the NSS (Network SuperServers, the backbone nodes) run an Interior Gateway Protocol (IGP) based on SPF (Shortest Path First). This protocol, based on IS-IS, floods routing information throughout the backbone and allows each node to compute optimal paths using the SPF algorithm.

At the edges, where regional networks attach to the backbone, the system uses the Exterior Gateway Protocol (EGP) in interior mode. EGP allows regional gateways to announce which networks they can reach. The NSS collects this information and redistributes it via EGP to other regional networks, subject to policy filtering. This two-protocol approach ensures that the backbone knows all reachable networks while allowing regional networks to control their routing policies.

Consistency is maintained through strict filtering rules and metrics. For example, routes learned from the ARPANET are marked with the ARPANET autonomous system number and are not redistributed into regional networks without special authorization. Metrics (path costs) are reconstituted at the backbone level rather than accepting metrics from regional networks, ensuring the backbone can make coherent path decisions.
sections.plainLanguage: The backbone routers gossip with each other about all the best paths inside the backbone. When a regional network wants to tell the backbone about its networks, the backbone listens via EGP and then tells other regions, but only if the routing policy allows it.

sections.title: Policy Enforcement and Regional Gateways
sections.content:
Each regional network attaches to the backbone through a gateway router and must follow strict rules to prevent routing problems. Regional networks must have unique Autonomous System (AS) numbers, which identify them to the backbone. The backbone validates all routing announcements based on both network number and AS number, triggering alarms at the Network Operations Center if an unauthorized AS tries to announce routes.

Regional backbones must not announce routes for subnets or internal networks they do not own; they announce only their own networks and those of their attached campuses. If a regional network announces a route with a metric of "128" (the fixed metric used by the backbone for EGP announcements), the regional gateway should treat that metric as a signal that the backbone did not have a more preferred path, not as an actual path cost.

The regional gateways may also announce a DEFAULT route internally if the EGP connection to the backbone is working, allowing campuses to reach everything via the backbone. The document includes technical requirements for the routing software in regional gateways, such as the ability to filter routes on a per-network basis and to override EGP routes with preferred internal paths.
sections.plainLanguage: Each town that connects to the highway has to follow the highway's rules: prove you are who you say you are, only announce your own roads, and trust the highway's routing directions unless you have a better path of your own.

sections.title: Legacy of the Architecture
sections.content:
RFC 1093 documents the NSFNET Backbone routing architecture as it existed in February 1989. The document is informational and describes the architecture and policies in effect at that time. The appendix includes example configurations for the "gated" routing daemon, showing how regional networks would configure the system in practice.

While the NSFNET itself has since been decommissioned, the concepts described—policy-based routing, AS-based filtering, separation of interior and exterior routing protocols, and metric management—remained influential in Internet routing design. The principles of routing policy enforcement through selective route filtering and metric adjustment are still used in today's Internet.
sections.plainLanguage: This is how a working research network actually did it in 1989. The NSFNET is gone now, but the ideas it tested are still in use on the Internet today.
